mainEntity.name: Is it normal for a dental implant to ache at night after many years?

acceptedAnswer.text: A dental implant that has functioned comfortably for a long period before developing nocturnal aching warrants professional assessment. Whilst some people notice increased implant sensitivity during periods of stress or illness, a new pattern of nighttime discomfort — particularly if it is persistent — could indicate changes in the peri-implant tissues, occlusal (bite) changes, or the onset of bruxism. It is not something to dismiss simply because the implant has been in place for a long time. A dental review can help determine whether any intervention is needed.

mainEntity.name: Could grinding my teeth at night damage my dental implant?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, habitual teeth grinding (bruxism) can place considerable mechanical stress on a dental implant, as implants lack the natural shock-absorbing periodontal ligament that natural teeth have. Over time, this can contribute to inflammation of the surrounding tissues, micro-movement at the implant–bone interface, and even hardware issues such as crown wear or screw loosening. If bruxism is suspected, your dentist may recommend a custom occlusal splint to help protect the implant. Suitability for this and any other intervention depends on clinical assessment.

mainEntity.name: Why does lying down make my implant feel worse?

acceptedAnswer.text: When you lie down, blood pressure to the head increases slightly compared to when you are upright. If any degree of inflammation is present in the tissues surrounding your implant, this positional change in blood flow can amplify discomfort. Additionally, lying down removes the daytime distractions that mask low-level pain signals, making them more perceptible. For upper jaw implants, sinus pressure changes associated with lying flat can also play a role. None of these possibilities can be confirmed without a professional clinical assessment.

mainEntity.name: Can poor oral hygiene cause my dental implant to hurt at night?

acceptedAnswer.text: Inadequate oral hygiene can allow plaque to accumulate around the implant site, which may trigger inflammatory changes in the gum tissue (peri-implant mucositis) or, over time, in the underlying bone (peri-implantitis). These conditions can cause discomfort that may be more noticeable at night. Improving your oral hygiene routine and attending professional hygiene appointments can help manage early-stage peri-implant inflammation. However, if symptoms are present, a dental professional should assess the implant to determine the appropriate course of action.

mainEntity.name: When should I be concerned about dental implant discomfort?

acceptedAnswer.text: Whilst mild, brief discomfort following dental procedures or during periods of stress is not always a cause for concern, you should consider contacting your dental practice if you experience: persistent or worsening aching around the implant, swelling or redness of the surrounding gum, bleeding when cleaning around the implant, a feeling of looseness, or any unpleasant taste or odour at the implant site. These symptoms may indicate a condition that benefits from early professional management. It is always better to seek timely advice rather than wait for symptoms to escalate.

mainEntity.name: Could a night guard help with my implant aching?

acceptedAnswer.text: A custom-fitted night guard is a clinically recognised approach to managing the effects of bruxism on dental implants and natural teeth. However, it is important to understand that its suitability and likely benefit depend on whether bruxism is actually the cause of your discomfort. Other factors — such as peri-implant inflammation, occlusal issues, or sinus-related discomfort — require different management strategies. Only a thorough clinical assessment by a qualified dental professional can identify the most appropriate course of action for your individual circumstances.
